blocks.text: 1. Iterations

blocks.alt: One batch processed is one iteration

blocks.text: Batch Size, the previous topic, controlled how many examples go into each batch. Iterations is the precise term for each individual weight update within an epoch, a genuinely essential companion concept covered in full depth throughout this topic.
One iteration equals one batch processed, one update applied, a genuinely simple, direct definition that ties together every concept already covered so far in this module.
2. The Precise Definition

blocks.alt: One forward and backward pass is one iteration

blocks.text: This connects back to one batch, one update, already covered in Batches. Processing a single batch and applying its resulting weight update is genuinely one iteration, the smallest unit of training progress.
This is the smallest unit of training progress, genuinely finer-grained than a full epoch, and the term used throughout the rest of this topic to describe individual steps of training.

blocks.text: 3. The Iterations-Per-Epoch Formula

blocks.alt: Dataset size divided by batch size gives iterations per epoch

blocks.text: This connects back to Batch Size, already covered in the previous topic. The number of iterations per epoch equals dataset size divided by batch size, a genuinely direct, simple calculation.
This is the exact same calculation already covered as batch size versus dataset size in the previous topic, now given its own precise name: the number of iterations that occur within a single epoch.
4. The Precise Hierarchy Of Terms

blocks.alt: An iteration builds up into an epoch, which builds up into a full training run

blocks.text: A genuinely important, precise hierarchy of terms emerges from everything already covered in this module. This connects back to Epochs and Batches, both already covered in their own dedicated topics.
An epoch contains many iterations, and each iteration processes exactly one batch, a genuinely clear, three-level structure: epochs contain iterations, and iterations process batches.
5. Calculating Total Training Iterations

blocks.alt: Iterations per epoch times the number of epochs gives total iterations

blocks.text: A genuinely useful, real practical calculation multiplies iterations per epoch, already covered in this topic, by the total number of epochs, already covered in its own topic.
This gives the genuinely total number of weight updates across the entire training run, a single number that captures the full scale of a given training configuration at a glance.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Total training iterations is a genuinely useful number for estimating training time and for configuring iteration-based Learning Rate Schedules, both covered further later in this topic and the next module.

blocks.text: 6. Logging And Monitoring At The Iteration Level

This connects back to monitoring performance across epochs, already covered in Epochs. Many training frameworks log loss and other metrics at the iteration level, not just per epoch, already covered as one option there.

This is a genuinely finer-grained view than epoch-level monitoring alone provides, revealing fluctuations and trends within a single epoch that epoch-level summaries alone would genuinely smooth over and hide.
7. The Connection To Learning Rate Schedules

blocks.alt: A learning rate schedule is tied to the iteration count

blocks.text: This connects back to Learning Rate Scheduling, already covered in the Backpropagation & Optimization module. Some schedules adjust the learning rate at every single iteration, not just every epoch.

This is a genuinely finer level of control than epoch-based scheduling alone allows, letting the learning rate change smoothly and precisely throughout training rather than only in coarse, once-per-epoch jumps.

blocks.text: 8. Iterations Versus Steps

blocks.alt: Iterations and steps are the same thing under different names

blocks.text: A genuinely important terminology note applies here. The word step is often used as a genuinely direct synonym for iteration, both referring to the exact same single batch-processed, single-update event already covered in this topic.

Different frameworks and papers sometimes use these two terms genuinely interchangeably, so recognizing that "step" and "iteration" typically mean the same thing avoids genuine confusion when reading different sources.
9. Recognizing When Thinking In Iterations Genuinely Helps

Comparing training runs with genuinely different batch sizes, already covered, is a direct case where iterations, already covered in this topic, give a genuinely fairer basis than epochs alone for comparing progress.

Setting a genuinely precise Learning Rate Schedule or logging frequency is another genuine case where iteration-level granularity, already covered, offers genuinely finer control than epoch-level alone.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates calculating iterations per epoch and total training iterations, tying together every concept already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
dataset_size = 5000
batch_size = 32     # already covered in the previous topic
num_epochs = 10      # already covered two topics prior

iterations_per_epoch = -(-dataset_size // batch_size)  # ceiling division, already covered as the last batch edge case
total_iterations = iterations_per_epoch * num_epochs

print(f"Dataset size: {dataset_size}")
print(f"Batch size: {batch_size}")
print(f"Iterations per epoch: {iterations_per_epoch}")
print(f"Total epochs: {num_epochs}")
print(f"Total training iterations: {total_iterations}")
print("\nEach one of these iterations represents exactly one batch processed and one weight update applied, already covered in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows how a genuinely small change in batch size can meaningfully shift the total number of iterations, directly connecting back to the batch size tradeoffs already covered in the previous topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: An iteration is one batch processed, resulting in exactly one weight update.
Iterations per epoch equals dataset size divided by batch size.
The hierarchy is precise: an epoch contains many iterations, each processing one batch.
Total training iterations equals iterations per epoch times the total number of epochs.
Many frameworks log metrics at the iteration level for a finer-grained view than epochs alone.
Some Learning Rate Schedules adjust the learning rate at every single iteration.
The word step is commonly used as a direct synonym for iteration.
Iterations give a fairer basis than epochs for comparing runs with different batch sizes.
